sections.heading: About Lord Krishna
paragraphs: Of all the divine incarnations in the vast tapestry of Hindu mythology, none has captured the human heart with quite the warmth, the beauty, and the multidimensional richness of Lord Krishna. He is the mischievous child of Vrindavan who stole butter and the hearts of all who saw him. He is the divine lover whose celestial flute calls every soul home. He is the warrior who stood beside Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra and delivered the immortal wisdom of the Bhagavad Gita. He is the cosmic statesman, the perfect friend, the teacher of teachers, the God who dances.

Krishna is among the most complete divine manifestations ever known to humanity — encompassing within his single form every quality that can be imagined in the Divine: love and wisdom, play and seriousness, tenderness and power, beauty and depth. The name Krishna itself means 'the one who attracts' or 'the dark one' — an allusion both to his famously dark complexion and to the irresistible gravitational pull he exerts on every soul that encounters him. He is also known as Govinda (one who gives joy to cows and the world), Gopala (protector of cows), Madhava (the sweet one), and by hundreds of other names, each capturing a different facet of his infinite being.

In the Hindu understanding, Krishna is not merely a historical figure or a mythological character. He is a living presence — an aspect of the Supreme Consciousness that is eternally accessible, eternally responsive, and eternally pouring out love into the universe. The Bhagavata Purana — one of the most beloved of all Hindu texts, devoted almost entirely to the life and teachings of Krishna — describes his birth, childhood, youth, and maturity in extraordinary and intimate detail, and for hundreds of millions of Hindus, reading or hearing these stories is itself a form of direct communion with the Divine.

sections.heading: Spiritual Significance of the Krishna Temple at the Ashram
paragraphs: The Krishna temple at the Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari Ashram is a space of extraordinary gentleness and sweetness. Amma's relationship with Krishna is one of the deepest threads in her spiritual life, and this intimacy is felt the moment one enters the temple precincts. The deity has been installed and consecrated with meticulous care, and the years of Amma's devotional worship have created an atmosphere that is simultaneously serene and alive — a quality that long-time visitors describe as palpable sweetness in the air, a sense of being held in something warm and benevolent.

In the broader context of the Ashram's mission, the Krishna temple is profoundly appropriate. Krishna is the patron deity of cows, and the Ashram's Goshala — home to over 300 cows, bulls, and calves — is in many ways a physical embodiment of Krishna's teachings. The Goshala is itself a form of Krishnacharana, a living worship of the divine cowherd. Visitors who sit in the Krishna temple after spending time in the Goshala often report a sense of deep coherence, as though the deity and the animals and the river and the sky are all part of a single, unified act of sacred attention.

sections.heading: The Bhagavad Gita and the Teachings of the Krishna Temple
paragraphs: One of the most significant aspects of any Krishna temple is its role as a living reminder of the Bhagavad Gita — the Song of the Lord, Krishna's discourse to Arjuna delivered on the battlefield of Kurukshetra and arguably the most important spiritual text in the Hindu tradition. The Gita addresses every dimension of the human condition: the nature of action and inaction, the relationship between the individual soul and the universal consciousness, the paths of devotion, knowledge, and selfless service, the meaning of duty, and the nature of liberation.

At the Ashram's Krishna temple, the Gita is not merely a text to be recited but a living practice to be embodied. The spirit of Nishkama Karma — action without attachment to results — is evident in everything the Ashram does, from its community feeding programmes to its care of the cows to its support for surrounding villages. To sit before Lord Krishna at this Ashram is to sit in the presence of a teaching that is actively being practised all around you, in every act of service that the Ashram community performs.

sections.heading: The Spiritual Advantages of Visiting the Krishna Temple
paragraphs: Worshipping at this temple carries spiritual benefits that operate on multiple levels simultaneously. On the level of the emotions, the Krishna temple offers the incomparable sweetness of Bhakti — devotional love. Krishna is the deity of the heart; he awakens in the worshipper the most elevated and purifying emotion available to a human being: pure, unconditional love for the Divine. Many devotees report that simply sitting before the Krishna deity and allowing themselves to be open to whatever arises produces a natural expansion of the heart — a softening of the defensive structures we habitually maintain, a welling up of gratitude and tenderness that feels simultaneously deeply personal and utterly impersonal.

On a mental level, the contemplation of Krishna's teachings — particularly the Gita's guidance on equanimity, on performing one's duty without attachment, on recognising the eternal Self beneath the changing appearances of life — produces a clarity and steadiness of mind that is among the most practically useful of all spiritual gifts. In a world of constant distraction and anxiety, the quality of equanimity that Krishna teaches and embodies is profoundly therapeutic. Those who spend regular time in contemplation at the Krishna temple often report improvements in their capacity to respond rather than react to life's challenges, a greater ability to hold difficulties without being overwhelmed by them.

On the deepest spiritual level, the Krishna temple at this Ashram — consecrated as it is by Amma's own profound identification with the Divine — offers the possibility of what the tradition calls Darshan: the direct beholding of the Divine in a form that is accessible to the human senses and the human heart. Darshan is not merely looking at a statue; it is a two-way encounter in which the divine gazes back at the devotee, and in that meeting, something shifts — subtly or dramatically — in the devotee's sense of themselves and their relationship to the cosmos.
